plan.contextChunk: This figure pairs two panels side by side to tie the circular and graphical pictures of the sine function together. At the left, drawn faintly in gray, is a unit circle crossed by its axes and by a fan of radii at the special angles. At the right is a Cartesian plot with a horizontal axis labeled x and a vertical axis labeled y ticked at 1, 0, and -1; a solid dark blue curve labeled y = sin(x) enters from the left with an arrowhead, passes through the origin, climbs to a peak of 1, and turns downward toward a second arrowhead. Four dashed orange vertical segments drop from the curve to x-axis ticks labeled pi/6, pi/4, pi/3, and pi/2, and four dashed teal horizontal lines run leftward from those same curve points, across the gap between panels, to matching heights on the gray circle. The teal connectors carry the comparison the figure is built for: the height of a point on the unit circle at a given angle is the value plotted above that angle on the graph. Reading the sine graph as a running record of height on the circle is what lets quadrant position account for the sign of the function.

interactionPlan.concept: The sine of an angle is the height (y-coordinate) of the corresponding point on the unit circle, so the graph of y = sin(x) is a running record of that height as the angle sweeps around the circle.
elements: Left panel: faint gray unit circle centered at origin with horizontal and vertical axes drawn as double-headed arrows
Left panel: gray fan of radii at the special angles (multiples of π/6 and π/4) crossing the circle
Left panel: highlighted dark-blue radius from center to the moving point on the circle at the current angle
Left panel: moving point on the circle with a small vertical drop segment to the horizontal axis showing its height
Right panel: Cartesian axes, horizontal axis labeled x with arrowheads, vertical axis labeled y with arrowheads
Right panel: y-axis tick labels 1, 0, and -1 with short tick marks
Right panel: x-axis tick marks labeled π/6, π/4, π/3, π/2 (extendable to π, 3π/2, 2π)
Right panel: solid dark-blue curve y = sin(x) with arrowheads at both ends, passing through the origin and peaking at 1
Right panel: curve label 'y = sin(x)' in blue near the peak
Right panel: four dashed orange vertical segments dropping from the curve to the labeled x-axis ticks
Dashed teal horizontal connector lines running from points on the sine curve leftward across the gap to the matching heights on the gray circle
Moving dark-blue tracer dot on the sine curve at the current angle
Readout label showing current angle x and value sin(x)
Optional shaded quadrant tint on the circle indicating whether the height is positive or negative

interactions.label: Angle x (radians)
interactions.teaches: Dragging the angle moves the circle point and the graph point together, so the learner sees that the graph's height at x is literally the circle point's y-coordinate.

interactions.label: Sweep 0 → π/2 and trace the curve
interactions.teaches: Watching the radius rotate while the curve is drawn in real time makes the sine graph read as a continuous recording of vertical height on the circle.

interactions.label: Show
interactions.teaches: Extending past π/2 shows the height shrinking and then going negative below the x-axis, so quadrant position on the circle explains the sign of sine.

demo_steps.title: One angle, two pictures
demo_steps.narration: At x = π/6 the radius points up and to the right; the teal connector carries the circle point's height straight across to the graph, where the curve sits at exactly that height above π/6.

demo_steps.title: Climbing through the special angles
demo_steps.narration: Drag on to π/4 and then π/3: the point rises on the circle and the tracer rises on the graph in step, with the dashed orange drop lines landing on the matching tick marks.

demo_steps.title: The peak at π/2
demo_steps.narration: At π/2 the radius points straight up, the circle point's height equals the full radius of 1, and the sine curve reaches its maximum value of 1.

demo_steps.title: Watch the record being written
demo_steps.narration: Play the quarter-turn sweep: the radius rotates from 0 to π/2 while the blue curve is drawn from the origin to the peak, one height at a time.

demo_steps.title: Past the peak: sign follows quadrant
demo_steps.narration: Open the view to a full revolution and drag into the third quadrant: the circle point drops below the horizontal axis and the curve dips below the x-axis by exactly the same amount.

interactionPlan.keyInsight: The sine curve isn't a separate object from the circle — it is the circle point's height plotted against the angle, so every feature of the graph (the rise to 1, the fall, the negative dip) is just where the point sits vertically on the circle.
interactionPlan.reconstructionNotes: Two panels side by side on a white field. Left: a light-gray unit circle with gray double-arrow axes through its center and a gray fan of radii at the π/6 and π/4 family of angles; the active radius and its endpoint are dark navy blue, with a thin drop line to the horizontal axis. Right: black double-arrow Cartesian axes, y labeled at top, x labeled at right, y-axis ticked and labeled 1 and -1 with 0 at the origin. The sine curve is a thick dark navy arc entering from the left through the origin, peaking at 1 above π/2 and bending down toward the right arrowhead; label 'y = sin(x)' in blue near the top right of the peak. Dashed orange verticals drop from curve points to x-axis ticks labeled π/6, π/4, π/3, π/2 in stacked fraction form. Dashed teal horizontals run from those curve points leftward across the gap between panels to the same heights on the circle — these teal lines are the visual argument and should stay prominent. Keep both panels on a shared vertical scale so a height of 1 on the circle lines up with y = 1 on the graph.

authoredContext:
Notice how the sine values are positive between 0 and π, which correspond to the values of the sine function in quadrants I and II on the unit circle, and the sine values are negative between π and 2π, which correspond to the values of the sine function in quadrants III and IV on the unit circle. See the figure.

Plotting values of the sine function

A side-by-side graph of a unit circle and a graph of sin(x). The two graphs show the equivalence of the coordinates.

Now let’s take a similar look at the cosine function. Again, we can create a table of values and use them to sketch a graph. The table lists some of the values for the cosine function on a unit circle.

Unchecked = first quadrant (0 → π/2), the view in the textbook figure.
⚠ Figure failed to load

discrepancies: The generated figure adds a persistent dynamic overlay absent from the source — highlighted radius, shaded sector, moving dots, a second navy drop line and a thick blue traced curve segment — which competes visually with the source's clean static composition at step 0.

Axis and tick labels ('1', '-1', '0', and the π/6, π/4, π/3, π/2 fractions) are rendered at ~10px in a 710px viewbox, appreciably smaller relative to the artwork than in the source, where the fractions are prominent; at inline size they are hard to read.

A sans-serif numeric readout block ('x = 0.52 rad (π/6)', 'sin(x) = height = 0.500') sits in the upper-left of the canvas; nothing like it appears in the source and it sits well away from the geometry it describes.

In the source the teal horizontal connectors visibly start at the circle point on the circle's arc and are accompanied by no navy drop line inside the circle; in the generated version the connectors are drawn at the circle point's x-position with an extra dashed vertical, slightly changing the read of the 'carry the height across' idiom.
The drawing is placed in the upper-left of a wide canvas leaving a large empty region below, so the figure reads smaller and less balanced than the source crop.
evaluation.notes: Structurally faithful recreation of the unit-circle-to-sine-graph figure with correct navy curve, teal horizontal carries, orange drop lines and π-fraction ticks, backed by genuinely pedagogical interactions (angle slider, quarter-turn sweep, full-revolution toggle, 5-step narration); main weaknesses are undersized axis/tick labels, an extra sans-serif readout block, and dynamic overlay clutter in the default state.

feedback.rationale: The concept and interaction structure are correct; remaining issues are implementation details—label sizing, extra readout block, overlay clutter in the default state, and canvas layout/balance.

discrepancies: The default state adds a navy radius, moving dot on the circle, a dashed drop line, and a tracer dot on the curve — none of these exist in the static source figure, so step 0 is not a pure drop-in replacement.

The sine curve is drawn further right (to roughly x ≈ 2.95, near π) than in the source, where the curve ends with its arrowhead shortly after the peak; the terminal arrow therefore sits much lower on the descending branch.
The three x-tick fraction labels (π/6, π/4, π/3) are crowded almost shoulder-to-shoulder at the chosen x-scale, reading as 'π π π / 6 4 3', whereas the source separates them more clearly.
The '0' origin label sits close to the descending left tail of the sine curve/axis and reads as slightly colliding with the artwork, unlike the clean placement in the source.
Small teal dots are added at the circle intersection points (not present in the source), and the circle spokes are lighter/thinner than the source's gray chords.
evaluation.notes: A faithful and well-composed reproduction of the unit-circle/sine-graph correspondence with correct teal horizontal connectors, orange vertical drops and tick fractions, backed by genuinely useful interactions (angle slider, sweep animation, full-revolution toggle, 5-step demo); weaknesses are minor label crowding at π/6–π/4–π/3, an origin label brushing the curve, and extra dynamic marks (radius, dots) present in the default view that the static source lacks.

Trim the default curve domain so the right-hand arrowhead sits just past the peak, matching the source's crop.
Consider muting or omitting the navy radius/tracer dot in the initial step-0 state (revealing them on first slider/step interaction) so the default render matches the static textbook figure exactly.
Make the circle's interior chords slightly darker/thicker to match the source's visible gray spokes.

feedback.rationale: Concept and interaction structure are correct; remaining issues are concrete rendering fixes (label crowding, curve domain crop, default-state extra marks, stroke weights) best handled by the generator.
